context: Reply to a reader interpreting the Heracles comparison
candidate: Thank you, Guillaume. I think that’s why this one was hard to write. I had to get far enough away from the layoff to stop asking what it said about me and start looking at what happened after it. Three months later, I have considerably more evidence to work with.
britt_feedback: No. I don’t want to make it about the layoff. I want to make it about how Heracles became much bigger than the Argo.
lesson: Follow the specific intellectual direction Britt names. Do not convert every personal metaphor into emotional processing.

context: Second attempt at the Heracles reply
candidate: That’s what I keep coming back to with Heracles. The Argo is one chapter in his story, but it’s not even close to the thing we remember him for. Jason gets the Golden Fleece. Heracles becomes one of the most enduring heroes in mythology. Sometimes the story you thought you were supposed to be part of just isn’t big enough for the story you’re going to have.
lesson: A true idea can still sound generated when it resolves too neatly into an inspirational lesson.

context: Third attempt after Britt rejected generic meaning-making
candidate: Thank you, Guillaume. I keep laughing at the comparison because the Argo was such a big deal in Jason’s story and basically a footnote in Heracles’s. He had a LOT of story left.
britt_feedback: No, I love the meaning and the length. You were resting on AI crutches.
lesson: When Britt rejects slop, do not automatically shorten. Preserve the depth and length she wants while replacing generic language with actual thought.

candidate_direction: Respond to the employee-branding argument rather than the fake CEO dialogue.
lesson: Choose the substantive argument Britt can credibly extend. Do not follow the source post's gimmick when a stronger operating implication is available.

britt_feedback: I edit the comments inline, to make it natural to mention the person inline so I show up as commenting on their post and mentioning them for more engagement.
lesson: Use LinkedIn readback as final authority. Place a real tagged mention naturally inside the sentence rather than treating the name as a salutation or engagement appendage.

context: Draft about using AI to learn from the behavior of top sellers
candidate: This is one of my favorite uses of AI. Go find the weird little thing your best person does that nobody taught them to do, figure out why it works, and make it easier for everyone else to do it too. Way more interesting than asking AI to invent the play from scratch.
revised_candidate: This is smart. Your best sellers have probably already figured out half the playbook. Go steal from them first.
lesson: A comment may need only the sharp conversational reaction. Do not use every relevant topic as an invitation to restate Britt's full thesis.

context: Draft response to a post proposing six changes to marketing because the old inbound model is breaking
britt_feedback: is that related to his post
lesson: A comment must visibly engage the actual claim or question in the source post. Topical adjacency is not enough, even when the adjacent point is true and on-brand.

context: Responding to a point Britt already agrees with
candidate_direction: Appreciate the point without bolting another operating-model argument onto it.
lesson: Not every comment needs to demonstrate the full body of expertise. Sometimes agreement becomes distinctive through concrete wording and taste.

britt_source: do we think this is the case for all sizes of companies?
lesson: When a source makes a universal GTM claim, test it against company size, maturity, ACV, sales motion, and category before agreeing.

context: Comment about the context agents need to make decisions
britt_feedback: Good points but not casual enough
revised_candidate: I think this is where the context conversation gets really fun. We spent years trying to cram everything into the CRM and then wondered why half the useful stuff still lived in people’s heads and random Slack threads. Agents kind of force the issue. If you want them making decisions, they need all that messy context too.
lesson: Preserve the substantive point, but write a comment like conversation rather than a miniature keynote. This replacement remains a candidate, not a published final.

context: Comment disagreeing that AI strategy itself must remain human
candidate: I’m less convinced that the strategy itself has to remain human. I think AI can be incredibly useful in building strategy when it has enough context. The part I wouldn’t hand over is accountability for the strategy. Somebody still has to decide whether it’s good, whether it reflects the business, and whether they’re willing to bet on it.
revised_candidate: I’m actually willing to let AI into the strategy part too. I use it to argue with me, poke holes in things, and make me consider options I wouldn’t have gotten to on my own. I just wouldn’t let it have the final vote.
lesson: A defensible distinction can still be slop when it sounds like a position paper. Ground the same idea in how Britt actually uses the technology and end conversationally. The replacement remains a candidate, not a published final.

context: Britt rejected a competent consultant case-study post because it did not match the content pattern she had deliberately established the prior week.
candidate_direction: Open with a client's GTM problem, show Britt diagnosing the hidden process defect, and end by teaching the operating-model lesson.
britt_feedback: But look at that formula we came up with last week. It's more like, you know, something where we're telling a story. It's very like, this is about me and this is about my career. This is about growth. And then it's like, you know, and so if I was going to do this again, you know, these are three things that I would do differently, right? Like didn't we learn that last week?
lesson: For current LinkedIn posts, make Britt the story rather than the consultant observing someone else's problem. The preferred sequence is something happened to Britt, the story reveals growth or changed judgment, and the ending names what she would do differently or what she learned. Expertise should emerge underneath the story instead of becoming the post's announced premise. This is a drafting rule, not proof that any assistant rewrite was published.

context: Britt corrected a response that had abstracted her experience into an enterprise buying-group lesson when the point she wanted was her own early-founder pattern of knowingly giving free advice to companies that could not afford her.
candidate_direction: Relate the source post to enterprise buying groups and account coverage.
britt_feedback: No, that's not what I mean. I mean, like, right after I started my business, I sat down with several companies that really could not afford me, and I knew they couldn't afford me, and I kept giving away free advice, and I really should have been like, Hey, um, no, I don't get paid in just equity, or referral bonuses only. Like, no. Yeah. Just no.
lesson: When Britt names a specific autobiographical and commercial point, keep that point. Do not upgrade it into a broader GTM lesson. Preserve the uncomfortable founder admission, the cash boundary, and her willingness to end with a blunt no. Any assistant rewrite remains a candidate until LinkedIn readback proves the published wording.
